title: How Docker Containers Actually Work — Explained Visually

sentences: You have probably heard that a container is like a lightweight virtual machine.
That is wrong, and the misunderstanding causes real production bugs.
A container is an ordinary Linux process.
It just cannot see most of the rest of the system, and it cannot consume more than its share of CPU and memory.
Let us prove it, and understand why it matters.
Scenario one. You deploy two services on the same EC2 instance without resource limits.
One service has a memory leak. An hour later, the other service starts crashing with out-of-memory errors, even though it is perfectly healthy.
This is a real incident pattern. The fix is cgroups, but first you need to understand what a container actually is.
Linux namespaces are the first half of the answer.
A namespace is a filter. Processes inside one namespace see only the resources inside it.
The PID namespace gives every container its own process table, so the main process is PID one inside the container, even though it has a different number on the host.
The net namespace gives it a private network stack: its own interfaces, routing table and ports.
The mnt namespace gives it its own filesystem view, which is where the container image comes in.
There are six namespace types in total. Docker sets all of them up when you run a container.
Namespaces hide things. cgroups limit things.
A control group is a kernel bookkeeping entry that tracks and caps CPU and memory use for a set of processes.
When you pass the memory flag to docker run, Docker writes that limit into a cgroup, and the kernel enforces it hard.
Without a limit, one leaking process can starve every other container on the host.
Always set memory and CPU limits in production. It is a one-line fix that prevents our scenario entirely.
The third piece is the filesystem.
A Docker image is a stack of read-only layers. Each instruction in your Dockerfile adds one layer.
When a container starts, Docker adds a thin writable layer on top. That layer is private to this container.
When the container writes a file that already exists in a lower layer, it copies the file up first. This is called copy-on-write.
This is why images are small and start fast, and why deleting a file in a later Dockerfile layer does not shrink the image.
Scenario two. Your image is two gigabytes and every build reinstalls all packages, even when you changed one line of code.
The reason is layer caching. Docker caches each layer by its content. The moment a layer changes, every layer above it is invalidated.
The fix: copy only your dependency manifest first, install packages, then copy the rest of the code.
One code change now invalidates only the last layer. A five-minute build drops to thirty seconds.
When you run docker run, four things happen in under a second.
Docker pulls the image layers if they are not already cached locally.
It creates a cgroup entry for the new container.
It sets up all six namespaces.
It starts your process inside that namespace-and-cgroup cage.
There is no boot sequence, no guest kernel, no hypervisor.
You can see the container as a process on the host with ps aux right now. The host is never hidden from itself.
Interviewers rarely ask for definitions. They ask you to compare containers and VMs under pressure.
Isolation: a VM has its own kernel; a container shares the host kernel, so a kernel exploit can in theory escape the container.
Startup: a VM boots in tens of seconds; a container starts in milliseconds because there is no boot sequence.
Overhead: a VM image carries a full OS; a container image is your application and its dependencies on top of shared layers.
Neither is strictly better. VMs win on isolation. Containers win on density and speed.
On the job, production Kubernetes clusters use both: VMs as nodes, containers as workloads.
Recap. Namespaces isolate. cgroups limit. Layered filesystems make images small and fast.
A container is a process with a filtered view of the system and a resource cap.
Always set resource limits. Order your Dockerfile so slow layers come first and change rarely.

A container is not a mini virtual machine.
It is a Linux process with three things applied to it.
Namespaces, so it cannot see the rest of the system.
cgroups, so it cannot consume more than its share of memory and CPU.
And a layered filesystem, so it starts in half a second.
No guest kernel. No boot. Just your process in a cage.
